stances.claim: Jesus Christ's five leadership qualities -- beginning with clear vision/mission, courage/conviction, and servant-leadership -- are as relevant and compelling today as they were 2,000 years ago.
Philippine political leaders -- who use pork barrels for patronage, seek personal credit, and make themselves centers of authority -- embody the exact opposite of Jesus's servant-leadership model.
stances.rhetorical_move: contemporary-political application of the Gospel teaching

notable_anecdotes: The pattern of Jesus's parables ending with questions -- Good Samaritan ('Which was neighbor?'), Forgiven Debtors ('Which was more grateful?'), Tenants ('What fate for them?') -- as a teaching method designed to make the listener discover truth for himself.

Jesus's 'Woe to scribes and Pharisees' rebuke: 'whitewashed tombs, beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones' -- the most rhetorically striking passage quoted in the column.

Jesus washing the apostles' feet: 'If I, who am Teacher and Lord, have washed your feet, then you, too, must wash each other's feet' -- the servant-leadership paradigm applied directly to Philippine public officials.
target_audience: Philippine political leaders measured against the servant-leadership standard
Business and civic leaders applying leadership frameworks
General readers seeking inspiration from Gospel leadership
register_markers: Contemporary-PH contrast embedded in theological reflection
decision_framework_signals: Apply Jesus's parable method: end with questions rather than directives -- good leaders make others discover truth for themselves
Apply the servant-leadership test to any public official: are they serving the people or using the people's resources to create personal obligation and patronage?
Apply the whitewashed-tombs test: does an official's public appearance match the ethical reality inside?
one_paragraph_summary: On Palm Sunday (May 1, 2011), Panganiban delivers Part 1 of a reflection on Jesus Christ as the eternal leader -- 'the same yesterday, today and tomorrow' -- identifying five leadership qualities of which he covers three. First, vision and mission: Jesus communicated His salvific mission differently to different audiences -- lofty and authoritative to disciples ('the greatest teaching of all time'), parables to non-disciples that ended with questions ('Which of these three was neighbor to the man?'; 'Which of them was more grateful?'; 'What fate do you suppose the owner has in store for them?') -- designed to make the listener discover truth for himself. Second, courage and conviction: in a world with no freedom of speech or dissent, Jesus mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, and an adulteress; acquired a reputation as 'a glutton and a drunkard'; and boldly denounced the scribes and Pharisees as 'whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones.' Third, servant-leadership: Jesus explicitly taught 'The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve' and demonstrated it by washing the apostles' feet -- contrasting sharply with Philippine political leaders who use pork barrel appropriations for personal patronage, and who make themselves the center of authority 'such that no business can be opened without their blessings and no employment can be secured without their recommendation.'
